cards.text: Paul, an apostle, is writing this letter to everyone in Rome who is loved by God (Romans 1:1, 7). He just said a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart (Romans 2:29). That raises a question: what's the advantage of being a Jew, or the value of circumcision?

cards.question: Paul says being a Jew still has an advantage, much in every way.

cards.text: Much in every way, Paul says. Then he names the first one on his list.

cards.question: What's the first advantage of being a Jew that Paul names?

answers.text: They were trusted with God's very words
They were spared from God's judgment
They were given every land on earth

cards.text: Then Paul asks a hard one. What if some of them did not have faith?

cards.question: If some of the people trusted with God's words don't have faith, does that cancel out God's faithfulness?

cards.text: Paul says, "Certainly not! Let God be true and every man a liar." Every man, friend, and that includes the stamper who told the dough "back in one minute" and came back after a NAP.

cards.question: Paul backs it up with a line from the Scriptures about God speaking and judging. How does God come out?

cards.text: Now Paul tries out a tricky idea, speaking in human terms, as he puts it. If our unrighteousness highlights God's righteousness, is God unjust to bring His wrath on us?

cards.question: Paul agrees that God would be unjust to bring His wrath on people whose unrighteousness highlights His righteousness.
Paul's reason: if God were unjust, how could He ___ the world?

cards.text: Paul tries the idea one more way, this time with "my falsehood." Same argument, new apron.

cards.question: Paul asks: if his lie made God's ___ shine even brighter, why would he still be condemned as a sinner?

cards.text: Follow that thinking all the way and you land on a line that some people slanderously claim Paul and others say.

cards.question: What's the line some people slanderously claim Paul and others say?

answers.text: Let us do evil that good may result
Let us obey so that we may be blessed
Let us rest so that God may work

cards.text: That's like burning a batch ON PURPOSE so the next one looks amazing. Paul's last word on it: "Their condemnation is deserved!"
Paul asks, "What then? Are we any better?" Then he answers, "Not at all," and says he's already made the charge about who's under sin.

cards.question: Paul says he's already made the charge. Who is under sin?

cards.text: Then Paul quotes the Scriptures: "There is no one righteous, not even one." I raised my mustache to say "What about..." and that verse said NOT EVEN ONE, Dorin.

cards.question: Paul's quote from the Scriptures says a few people still seek God.
Paul's quote keeps going about everyone. What have all of them done?

cards.text: Then the quotes zoom in on the body: their throats are open graves, their tongues practice deceit, and the venom of vipers is on their lips. Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness too, and friend, that viper venom is NOT lip balm.

cards.question: Throats, tongues, lips and mouths: this part of Paul's quotes is all about what people say.

cards.text: From the mouth, the quotes go all the way down to the feet: "Their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery lie in their wake, and the way of peace they have not known."

cards.question: First Paul's quotes picture what people say. Now, with the feet, they picture what people ___.

cards.text: Paul's last quote looks at the eyes: "There is no fear of God before their eyes."

cards.question: Paul strings all these quotes from the Scriptures together to show that only some people are under sin.

cards.text: Now Paul says something we know: whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law.

cards.question: Paul says the law speaks to those under it. Why, according to Paul?

answers.text: So the whole world is accountable to God
So those under it can boast in it
So the Greeks are left out of it

cards.text: Every mouth silenced. EVERY mouth, even Mags, and Mags was the loudest voice in the whole kitchen. Then Paul lands it: "no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law."

cards.question: Paul says the law merely brings awareness of ___.

cards.text: That's the law, friend: a mirror that shows you the flour on your face. It can't wipe it off.

findings.problem: The opening card uses Romans 1:1 and 1:7 for who Paul is and who the letter is written to, and Romans 2:29 for context. Its verses field says "Romans 2:29-3:1". That range is narrower than what the card uses because it leaves out 1:1 and 1:7. It also starts before the stop's range of Romans 3:1-8. Following the citation rule literally would give "Romans 1:1-3:1", which covers more than two chapters for one opening card.
findings.question: How should a story card's verses field cite outside-passage context, such as the letter's author and readers or the verse right before the passage? Should the field cover every verse the card uses, even outside the passage and the stop's range? Or should it cite only the passage verses and leave outside references in the text?

findings.problem: The wrong answer "They were given every land on earth" is silly and nobody would believe it. It doesn't match the tone of the other two answers, so the choice becomes a two-way pick.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Several details in Romans 3:11-12 are never told on any card: no one understands, all have together become worthless, and there is no one who does good, not even one. Card 4 asks only about seeking God, and card 5 asks only about turning away. The baker never hears the rest of the charge.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: This true or false card asks again what stop 2 card 2 already settled: Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin (Romans 3:9). It recaps instead of moving the passage forward. It also cites a wide range, Romans 3:9-18, for an answer that comes from 3:9.

rule.text: Ask about the moments that move the passage forward and the details the baker needs to understand it.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: "Every mouth silenced." / "EVERY mouth, even Mags, and Mags was the loudest voice in the whole kitchen." / "Then Paul lands it: ...". It also carries two beats from two verses, the silenced mouths in 3:19 and the line about not being justified in 3:20.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Cards 10 and 12 are bare restatements of the verse, with no Papa Dorin voice: "Paul's last quote looks at the eyes: ..." and "Now Paul says something we know: ...". Card 8 is also just a frame around a quote. Together these cards read like a plain retelling, not Papa Dorin telling the passage.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
